Iterated Weighted Least Squares

Source: R/iwls.R
iwls.Rd

Configures the scoring step with which statmod() fits the smooth block, and returns it as an object to pass as inner_optimizer. This is the default, so statmod(...) and statmod(..., inner_optimizer = iwls()) fit the same model; call it by name to change the solver, the budget, the stopping rule or the constants of the loop.

The matrix that the step inverts is chosen by the argument inner_information of statmod() (see information_objects), and not by iwls(): the step is a Newton method on whatever curvature the objective offers. Every argument of iwls() has a default, and the object carries no data, so one iwls() can be passed to any number of fits.

Usage

iwls(
  solver = solve_qr(),
  maxit = 1000L,
  tol = 1e-06,
  criterion = NULL,
  step_halving = 30L,
  decrement_limit = 1e-06,
  switch_after = 10,
  switch_rate = 0.5
)

# S3 method for class 'Iwls'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

solver

The factorization with which each step is solved, an object that inherits from IwlsSolver: solve_qr() (the default), solve_svd() or solve_chol(). iwls_solvers compares the three and gives their tolerances.

maxit

The iteration budget, a single positive whole number.

tol

The stopping tolerance on the score per observation, a single positive number.

criterion

An optimizers7 criterion object driving the loop in place of tol, or NULL for the built-in rule.

step_halving

The number of halvings tried after the full step before a step is abandoned, a single non-negative whole number. The line search tries the full step and then at most step_halving halved steps, so 0 tries only the full step.

decrement_limit

The value under which the Newton decrement is read as small by the built-in stopping rule, a single positive number. The default is 1e-6.

switch_after

The iteration after which a run settled on the expected information from auto_info() continues on the observed information, a single positive number; Inf never switches. The default is 10.

switch_rate

The ratio of consecutive scores above which two consecutive steps count as a slow contraction of Fisher scoring, a single number or NA, which never counts a run as slow. The default is 0.5.

x

An Iwls() object.

...

Unused.

Value

An Iwls() object holding the settings given and no data. Its hessian is an unsettled auto_info() until statmod() settles the argument inner_information.

The name

The name abbreviates iterated weighted least squares. The word iterated already implies the re-weighting, so the abbreviation irls is not used.

The curvature

The step inverts the matrix that inner_information of statmod() selects. With distributions7::expected_info() it inverts the expected information, which is Fisher scoring, and with distributions7::observed_info() the observed Hessian, which is Newton. The expected information is positive definite wherever the family is regular, so Fisher scoring takes usable steps from a poor start where Newton's matrix may be indefinite; Newton converges faster near the optimum. An explicit choice is the only matrix that the step uses: the observed information is never replaced by the expected one.

The default inner_information = auto_info() is settled against the family when the fit starts. The expected information is used where the family writes it exactly and at an acceptable cost. Otherwise the observed information is used, and the expected information takes the step where the observed step, after the repair of an indefinite matrix, finds no acceptable point. A trial point whose objective raises an error is read as rejected. The fit records the settled choice, so fit@methods$smooth shows which curvature ran.

On a family that auto_info() settles on the expected information, a run continues on the observed information as soon as Fisher scoring contracts the score slowly, which means that each of two consecutive ratios of the score is above switch_rate, and at the latest after switch_after scoring steps. Fisher scoring converges only linearly near the mode wherever the two informations differ there, which they do whenever the dispersion has an equation of its own, whereas Newton's step converges quadratically.

Where the stopping rule is met, the run takes one more full step. The step uses the observed information if the choice was settled on the expected information from auto_info() and has not yet switched, and otherwise the information that the run is using. The marginal criterion carries \(\log\lvert K(\beta)\rvert\), which is not stationary in \(\beta\), so a mode left short by \(\delta\) enters it at first order; a warm-started fit whose score is already under the rule would stop without moving and leave the criterion out by an amount linear in the outer step. The extra step takes the error to second order. It is kept unless it raises the objective by more than a relative \(10^{-8}\): a sufficient-decrease test at a point already under the rule would accept or reject by the last bits, and the criterion would jump between nearby hyperparameters.

The method carried by distributions7::expected_info() and auto_info() is passed to distributions7. With method = NULL, the default, the closed form of the family is used where the family has one (distributions7::expected_hessian_exact() records which case a family is in), and distributions7::expect_opg(), the outer product of the observed scores, which costs one gradient, otherwise. An object is used for every family, also for one that has the closed form. distributions7::expect_integrate() and distributions7::expect_mc() evaluate the expectation itself (a sum over the support or a quadrature, or simulated draws) and cost much more inside a loop that rebuilds the curvature at every iteration. distributions7::expected_derivative_methods compares the three. The price of the cheap matrix is paid in variance and not in the answer: the score is exact, so a scoring step driven by any positive definite matrix reaches the same stationary point, and the outer product is positive semidefinite by construction, whereas the observed Hessian need not be. The information behind a standard error is chosen separately; see vcov_method.

The solver

The step solves \((X'WX + S)\delta = X'g - S\beta\), and the argument solver selects the method.

solve_qr()

a QR of the augmented design \([\sqrt{W}X;\ \mathrm{chol}(S)]\), and the default. Forming \(X'X\) squares the condition number, and the design of a break-point term is bounded only to \(\epsilon^{-1/2}\) by construction, so that squaring it exhausts double precision.

solve_svd()

a singular value decomposition of the same augmented design. It reports a numerical rank where a deficient block would make a Cholesky fail.

solve_chol()

a Cholesky factor of the penalized information \(X'WX + S\), assembled without the augmentation. The information is formed explicitly, so the condition number is squared.

solve_qr() and solve_svd() need a square root of the per-observation curvature and of the penalty. Where either does not exist, the step uses the assembled information, as solve_chol() does. iwls_solvers compares the three and gives the tolerances that each one takes.

The stopping rule

A scoring step is not an optimizer and carries its own loop, but the rule that ends the loop belongs to the caller.

With criterion = NULL, the default, the built-in rule applies. The rule is met when the score per observation \(\max_j \lvert g_j \rvert / n\), taken over the free coordinates, is below tol and the Newton decrement \(g^\top (H+S)^{-1} g / 2\) is at most decrement_limit. The decrement is in log-likelihood units and does not depend on the scale of the response. When the loop ends without meeting the rule, the dimensionless reading of iwls_score() can relabel the stopped run as converged. Any optimizers7 criterion may drive the loop instead. It replaces the whole built-in rule, including the decrement condition and the dimensionless reading, and tol is then not read, so passing both is an error.

The state that a criterion receives is the one that optimizers7::crit_met() documents. In this loop the state has three properties:

  • Its gradient is the score per observation, the quantity that the built-in rule compares with tol. The threshold of optimizers7::crit_grad(t) therefore applies to the same quantity as tol = t and has the same meaning at \(n = 10\) and at \(n = 10^7\).

  • Its f_new is the penalized objective, the negative penalized log-likelihood, not divided by the sample size, which is the scale on which the penalty is added. A rule that reads the absolute value of the objective therefore depends on the sample size; a rule that reads its relative change does not.

  • On the first iteration f_old and x_old are NULL, because there is no previous point, so a rule reading a change returns FALSE there by construction.

A criterion that needs a quantity that the step does not compute is rejected at construction. A stationarity measure is an example: it belongs to the derivative-free methods, and a rule that requires one would remain in the loop without ever being met.

The constants of the loop

Three constants of the loop are arguments. decrement_limit is the value under which the built-in rule reads the Newton decrement as small (default 1e-6, three orders under the reading that the outer search uses to decide whether a criterion is usable). switch_after is the iteration after which a run settled on the expected information continues on the observed one (default 10; Inf never switches). switch_rate is the ratio of consecutive scores above which two consecutive steps count as a slow contraction (default 0.5; NA never counts one). The last two are read only when inner_information is settled from auto_info() on the expected information.

See also

statmod() for the argument inner_information and for where the object is passed, information_objects and iwls_solvers for the matrix and the solver, iwls_score() for the built-in rule's final verdict, optimizers7::crit_grad() for the criteria that can replace it.

Examples

iwls()
#> iwls: qr
#>   maxit 1000, tol 1e-06

# This call solves through an SVD, which reports a numerical rank where a
# deficient block would make a Cholesky fail.
iwls(solver = solve_svd())
#> iwls: svd
#>   maxit 1000, tol 1e-06

# This call uses an optimizers7 stopping rule in place of tol. The
# gradient in the state that the rule receives is the score per
# observation, as for tol.
iwls(criterion = optimizers7::crit_any(optimizers7::crit_grad(1e-8),
                                       optimizers7::crit_rel_obj(1e-12)))
#> iwls: qr
#>   maxit 1000, gradient (max-norm) < 1e-08 or |df| < 1e-12 (relative)

# The matrix is chosen in statmod(): this is Newton, on the observed
# information.
set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(120, -2, 2))
dd$y <- sin(1.4 * dd$x) + rnorm(120, sd = 0.3)
G <- distributions7::gaussian1_distrib()
fit <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 8)), G, dd,
               inner_optimizer = iwls(solver = solve_svd()),
               inner_information = distributions7::observed_info())
fit@methods$smooth
#> iwls: svd, observed information
#>   maxit 1000, tol 1e-06

# Both at once is an error: tol would not be read.
try(iwls(tol = 1e-8, criterion = optimizers7::crit_grad(1e-8)))
#> Error : 'tol' and 'criterion' both set the stopping rule: pass one.
#>   'tol' belongs to the built-in rule, which a criterion replaces.
